---
title: "A round in IMAG"
---

## The firm, the funds, the clients

You are fund manager at Asterion Capital, an asset manager whose founders are stepping back. The firm runs
**one fund per client type** and manages a total of up to four different funds, which can be either Conservative, Conservative (ESG), Dynamic, or Dynamic (ESG). Each fund has its own clients, its own benchmark and its own fees. The client card observable in the "Clients" section of the game tells you the home market, the risk-aversion bracket, the limits and the currently set fees of each fund. Fees can be adjusted each round, but the client does not change. The game does not allow you to change the fund type or the client type.

Asterion measures everything in **US dollars**. Assets in other currencies are held unhedged, and the game offers no way to hedge them. This creates currency risk, which is part of the risk you manage. The game does not allow you to change the currency of a fund.

The investable universe is 180 assets in four asset classes (government bonds, corporate bonds,
equities, alternatives) and five currencies (USD, GBP, EUR, CHF, JPY). Alternatives exist in USD
only. A **market segment** is one asset class in one currency, e.g. "EUR / Corporate bonds". 

<!-- Can the money market be considered a fifth asset class? It is not a tradeable asset and you once told me that you do not allow it. And even if it is an asset class wouldn't we only be able to hold USD so only one cash position not 5?-->
Together with the money market this gives 21 **positions** hold by each portfolio (money market, government bonds, corporate bonds and
equities in each of the five currencies, plus commodities). The strategic benchmark (or Strategic Asset Allocation) is defined on the 16 positions without the money market. In the optimal portfolio there is no cash position, as cash is a tactical decision of the player, not a strategic position.

## What the game measures

Three things drive assets under management (AuM), the amount of money available to the fund: 

1. **Risk-adjusted performance against the benchmark.** The benchmark of each fund is its
   strategic allocation. The game's Analyst page attributes your return against it (currency,
   asset class, industry, maturity, factors) and compares your strategic allocation with the
   optimal allocation held in the game's parameters.
2. **Client satisfaction.** Surveys ask whether the fund is managed the way the client expects:
   inside the limits, with the right amount of risk, with the required sustainability. A fund held
   far from what the client expects loses clients at once.
3. **Fees.** Higher fees turn clients away but raise revenue; clients tolerate fees better when
   their risk-adjusted return is good. Dynamic clients respond to marketing and accept higher
   fees; conservative clients want them low and transparent.

AuM directly drives the firm's profit, which is the sum of the fees of all funds multiplied by their AuM. Because of this the goal of each fund manager should be to grow AuM, which is done by maximizing risk-adjusted performance against the benchmark, keeping clients satisfied and charging fees that are appropriate.

The instructor picks the winning criterion (Sharpe ratio, alpha, information ratio, cumulative
shareholder return of the firm). Whatever it is, it runs through the same three channels.

## The decision flow

The game suggests an order, and this book follows it. Each step is one chapter.

| Step | Page in the game | What you decide | Tool | Chapter |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Clients | Read the client: the rules, the risk aversion bracket, the limits | Client card, this book | 2 |
| 2 | Course dataset | Read the market: statistics and correlations of the benchmark positions | App, station 1 | 3 |
| 3 | Investment strategy → Strategic allocation | The strategic allocation of each fund, its benchmark for the whole game | App, station 2 | 4 |
| 4 | Economic outlook, Analyst | Turn the outlook into views on expected returns | App, station 3 | 5 |
| 5 | Investment strategy → Tactical allocation | The tactical allocation for this round | App, station 4 | 6 |
| 6 | Investment strategy → Automation preferences, Markets | How tactical weights become positions; the ESG floor; asset-level decisions | Game | 7 |
| 7 | Clients → Fees, Projections, Decision checklist | Fees, check projections, submit as team | Game | 8 |
| 8 | Results, Analyst | Read performance, attribution, satisfaction; feed it back | Game | 9 |

Steps 1 to 3 are done once, in the first round, and the result stays for the whole game: the
client does not change and the strategic allocation is the benchmark. Steps 4 to 8 repeat every
round.

::: {.callout-tip title="The allocation app"}
The course provides a Shiny app available at <https://inno.uni.li/apps/invest/> with four stations that mirror steps 2 to 5. It runs on the course
dataset: the full history of the 21 positions, monthly, in dollars, with the money market left out
of the benchmark by default. Appendix A is its reference.
The app does not talk to the game; you read numbers off the app and type them into the game.
:::

## Rounds, practice rounds, teams

A round is typically one quarter. Before the first round, the course instructor may allow up to three practice rounds. In a practice round you can make decisions and see the results, but the market does not move and your decisions do not carry over. The purpose is to learn how to use the platform and how to make decisions. After the practice rounds, the market resets and the first round begins with the decisions of the first practice round as starting decisions. Nothing else carries over.

<!-- Should we add images to show where the different sections are in the platform? -->

Each team member has a **Student Decision Area**; the round is scored on the **Team Decision
Area**. Work in your own area, then *Copy as team's decisions*; a copy overwrites the team area
without backup. Appoint a round CEO who submits, and rotate the role.

Between rounds the game moves your holdings with the market and with fund flows, and, if
automation is on, rebalances them to your tactical weights (Chapter 7). The strategic allocation
is not touched by this; it is a benchmark, not a holding.

## The round on one page

1. Round 1 only: read the client (Ch. 2), read the market (Ch. 3), set and fix the strategic
   allocation of every fund (Ch. 4), enter it on the Investment strategy page.
2. Set the ESG floor for the ESG funds in Automation preferences (Ch. 7).
3. Read the Economic outlook; write down your views with a confidence (Ch. 5).
4. Run the tactical station for every fund; enter the tactical allocation; check the projected
   tracking error and information ratio (Ch. 6).
5. Decide whether to touch asset-level positions; usually not in the first rounds (Ch. 7).
6. Set fees; read Projections; copy to the team area before the deadline (Ch. 8).
7. After the deadline: Results and Analyst; revise your γ estimate and your views (Ch. 9).
